title: Reading a function signature
intro: A function's signature is everything before its body: the name, the parameters, the result type, and any conditions on generic types. In Rust it packs in a lot, because it also says what a function may change, whether it can fail, and what its generic types must be able to do. This page reads real signatures from the standard library, piece by piece, and shows the `use`, `pub` and `::` syntax that finds them.

coming_from.go: `func Largest[T cmp.Ordered](list []T) T` becomes `fn largest<T: PartialOrd>(list: &[T]) -> &T`: the type parameter and its bound go in `<>` after the name, and the result follows `->`. Go's `int` is 32 or 64 bits by platform (64 on the runner), so write `i64` to pin it, or `isize` to follow the platform. The `&` in `&[T]` borrows the list (a view of its items) instead of taking it.
coming_from.kotlin: `fun <T : Comparable<T>> largest(list: List<T>): T` becomes `fn largest<T: PartialOrd>(list: &[T]) -> &T`. The type parameter moves after the name, `->` replaces the `:` before the result, and the `&` in `&[T]` borrows the list (a view of its items) instead of taking it.
coming_from.python: A hinted signature like `def largest(items: Sequence[T]) -> T` becomes `fn largest<T: PartialOrd>(list: &[T]) -> &T`. The interpreter ignores hints; the Rust compiler checks every piece before the program runs. `PartialOrd` plays the part of the `Comparable` protocol in the main program, and a call with a type that lacks it is a compile error.
coming_from.typescript: `function largest<T extends number | string>(list: T[]): T` becomes `fn largest<T: PartialOrd>(list: &[T]) -> &T`. `extends` turns into a colon, and the bound names an ability (a trait) such as comparing with `>`, not a union of types. Breaking the bound is a compile error, as it is in TypeScript.
coming_from.java: `static <T extends Comparable<T>> T largest(List<T> list)` becomes `fn largest<T: PartialOrd>(list: &[T]) -> &T`. The type parameter follows the name, `extends` turns into a colon, and the result follows `->`. The `&` in `&[T]` borrows the list (a view of its items) instead of taking it.
coming_from.csharp: `static T Largest<T>(IReadOnlyList<T> list) where T : IComparable<T>` becomes `fn largest<T: PartialOrd>(list: &[T]) -> &T`. Rust has a `where` clause too, but a short bound sits inside the `<>`. The result follows `->`, and the `&` in `&[T]` borrows the list (a view of its items).
coming_from.c: C has no generic functions (`_Generic` only chooses between per-type ones), so `int largest_int(const int *list, int n)` is written once per type. Rust writes one `fn largest<T: PartialOrd>(list: &[T]) -> &T`: the `[T]` slice knows its own length, and `&` is a reference, a pointer the compiler checks.
coming_from.cpp: `template <std::totally_ordered T> const T& largest(const std::vector<T>&)` becomes `fn largest<T: PartialOrd>(list: &[T]) -> &T`. A trait bound is the nearest thing to a C++20 concept, but a type meets a trait only by declaring it. `&T` is like `const T&`, and `&[T]` accepts an array, a `Vec` or part of one.

notes: A generic function lists its type parameters in `<>` after its name. `T: PartialOrd` is a bound: it says a `T` must be able to be compared with `>` and `<`, and `+` joins several bounds.
`&T` is a borrowed look at a `T`, `&mut T` a borrow that may change it, and a bare `T` hands the value over (small types such as integers are copied instead). The signature tells you which.
The result follows `->`. `Option<&T>` means "maybe a reference", and `Result<T, E>` means "a `T`, or an error `E`", so a signature says whether a call can come back empty or fail.
Read a long signature in this order: the name, the parameters, the result, and the bounds last. `::` walks a path such as `std::cmp::max`, and `use` brings a name in so you can write it short.

gotcha.title: Comparing a type that has no bound
gotcha.looks_fine: In Python, TypeScript and C++ a function can compare two values of a type `T` it knows nothing about: `if item > best`. The check comes later, or never, so the code looks complete.
gotcha.rust_sees: Inside `largest<T>`, `T` is any type at all, and a type is not promised to have `>`. Rust checks the body against what the signature promises, so the signature must say it: `T: PartialOrd`.
gotcha.why: Rust reads a generic function once, as written, and refuses anything its bounds do not allow. The error comes with a `help:` that spells out the bound to add. Go, Kotlin, Java and C# refuse the same code and need their own spelling (`cmp.Ordered`, `Comparable<T>`, `IComparable<T>`); TypeScript, Python and C++ accept it, as the outputs show.

go.says: Go refuses: with `[T any]`, `>` is not allowed, because `any` includes types that cannot be ordered. Go needs `[T cmp.Ordered]`, which plays the part of `T: PartialOrd` but is a fixed list of built-in types; a Rust trait can be implemented for your own types too.
go.error:
# command-line-arguments
./main.go:10:6: invalid operation: item > best (type parameter T cannot use operator >)

kotlin.says: Kotlin refuses: an unbounded `T` has no `>`. Write `<T : Comparable<T>>`.

python.says: Python prints the same. Nothing in `largest` says what it needs: `>` is tried on whatever arrives, and a list that cannot be ordered, such as `[3, "nine", 4]`, raises a `TypeError` only when that call runs.

typescript.says: TypeScript compiles this under `strict` and prints the same: it asks only that both sides of `>` have the same type, not that the type can be ordered. So `largest` on objects compiles and quietly returns the first one. The `extends number | string` in the main program is what makes it safe.

java.says: Java refuses: `>` works only on numeric types, so a generic needs `T extends Comparable<T>` and `compareTo`.

csharp.says: C# refuses (CS0019): add `where T : IComparable<T>` and call `CompareTo`.
csharp.error: Program.cs(9,13): error CS0019: Operator '>' cannot be applied to operands of type 'T' and 'T'

c.says: C prints the same. It has no generic functions, so there is no `T` to leave unbounded: you write one function per type, as the main program does.

cpp.says: C++ compiles and prints the same. An expression that depends on `T`, such as `>`, is checked when the template is used with a type; the page shows the error for a type with no `>`. A C++20 `requires` clause or concept states the bound up front, as Rust does.

python.code:
from typing import Any, Protocol, Sequence, TypeVar


class Comparable(Protocol):
    def __gt__(self, other: Any) -> bool: ...


T = TypeVar("T", bound=Comparable)


def largest(items: Sequence[T]) -> T:
    best = items[0]
    for item in items:
        if item > best:
            best = item
    return best


numbers = [3, 9, 4]
words = ["pear", "fig", "apple"]
print("largest number:", largest(numbers))
print("largest word:", largest(words))
